item.title: 25 Years After 9/11, Trump Personifies a Nation Moving On
item.description:
Of all of America’s five living presidents, none was closer to ground zero on the day that hijacked planes smashed into the World Trade Center than Donald J. Trump. But on the 25th anniversary of the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, none will be farther away.

Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joseph R. Biden Jr. are all scheduled to be in New York on Friday to mark the moment. But Mr. Trump, the only native New Yorker among them, will be some 200 miles south at the Pentagon, where, unlike at ground zero with its tradition of silence, he will be allowed to give a speech.

The disparate images will be stark and telling: four presidents of both parties standing together where the twin towers fell, four presidents whose time in office was shaped to one extent or another by the war on terrorism that gripped the nation for so long. And then the sitting president honoring the occasion at another attack site, estranged from his predecessors and governing at a time when fear of foreign attack has receded into the background of American life.

With the distance of a quarter century, Mr. Trump’s presidency has moved past the days when terrorism drove the agenda. Just as memories of Pearl Harbor lingered long after World War II ended, the memories of Sept. 11 remain powerful long after the death of Osama bin Laden. But the country and its politics have moved on.

The threat matrix delivered to the Oval Office starting after Sept. 11 now looks different than it used to. Domestic terrorism has become the more pressing concern, whether it be the mob assault on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, the assassination of the conservative leader Charlie Kirk last year or various antisemitic attacks on synagogues.

Mr. Trump has shifted the definition and scope of the war on terrorism. He has categorized drug cartels as a terrorist threat as he bombs boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. He has identified left-wing extremism as a terrorist threat, while ignoring right-wing extremism. And he has gone to war with Iran, one of the most prolific state sponsors of terrorism, though he frames that as a campaign to stop Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon more than one meant to destroy its proxy network.

“You don’t hear President Trump talk about terrorism all that much unless they’re attaching it to issues at the border or transnational crime,” said Nick Rasmussen, who served in major counterterrorism roles under Mr. Bush, Mr. Obama, Mr. Trump and Mr. Biden. “It’s not as if they’re focused on the threat aspects of the terrorism issue. I think they’re more focused on defining that with which they are politically seized with in the frame of a terrorism problem.”

Mr. Rasmussen, who was the director of the federal government’s National Counterterrorism Center through the first year of Mr. Trump’s first term and is now at the McCain Institute in Washington, said cuts and reorganizations have cost the government much expertise and resources. “I worry about the hollowing out of our institutions,” he said.

Daniel Byman, the director of the terrorism program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the issue is no longer an organizing principle the way it was under past presidents. “That kind of day-to-day focus on counterterrorism that was driving the president’s schedule and senior leaders just isn’t there,” he said.

To some extent, that reflects the success of years of bipartisan efforts after Sept. 11 to prevent another mass-casualty event of that magnitude, a victory that would have been unthinkable on Sept. 12 when another major attack was widely expected. That has allowed presidents understandably to turn to other priorities. But it always leaves the question of whether the country’s political leadership risks growing complacent.

“When people ask me, are we safer today, my answer is no,” said Bruce Hoffman, a Georgetown scholar who has studied terrorism for five decades. “Twenty-five years ago, we had just one terrorist group to focus on and that was Al Qaeda. Today, we have Al Qaeda and ISIS and their branches. We have the Iranian terror network, domestic terrorists.”

“Every expansion of our definition of terrorism means resources have to be more thinly sliced,” he added. “Are we drifting back into a 1990s mind-set is always my concern.”

Americans today are more afraid of one another than they are of foreign terrorists. A survey by Reuters and Ipsos this week found that only 20 percent considered foreign terrorism the biggest threat to average Americans compared with 33 percent who cited domestic terrorism and 42 percent who picked random violence like mass shootings. Asked which ideology-driven threats were bigger, 61 percent said domestic extremists versus 34 percent who said those from overseas.

Most jihadist plots in the United States are actually carried out by individuals who may be inspired by overseas groups but have no direct connection to them. Of 129 attacks and plots in the United States over 20 years, just 23 involved known contact with an international terrorist organization, according to a study by Mr. Byman’s center last year.

“Twenty-five years later, the U.S. has largely redefined what the issue of terrorism is,” said Philip D. Zelikow, a senior fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution who served as executive director of the bipartisan commission that investigated the Sept. 11 attacks and later as counselor to Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice.

For years, America was caught in a global conflict, then sought to extract itself as it pulled troops out of Iraq and Afghanistan, he said. “Our major military interventions since 2024 did not reflect a strategic decision to re-engage the great conflict within the Islamic world,” Mr. Zelikow said. “We don’t have a recognizable strategy to influence the outcome of that struggle.”

Instead, the Trump administration has focused its efforts on what it calls an America First approach. The administration’s counterterrorism strategy, released in May, identified three major threats: “narcoterrorists and transnational gangs,” “legacy Islamist terrorists” and “violent left-wing extremists, including anarchists and antifascists.”

“We face new categories and combinations of violent actors that make the established ways of doing counterterrorism insufficient or obsolete,” the strategy said. “We face a multiplicity of deadly threats from terror groups and nonstate actors often secretly supported by governments who wish to undermine us.”

The strategy had a sharply partisan tone, repeatedly attacking Mr. Biden, saying that “real threats were ignored or underplayed” while his administration promoted a “globalist left-wing cultural hegemony.” Stephen Miller, the president’s deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, has sought to focus on leftist extremism. After Mr. Kirk’s murder last year, he declared that “the Democrat Party is not a political party. It is a domestic extremist organization.”

This all represents quite a journey for Mr. Trump, who was himself a registered Democrat on the sunny autumn day 25 years ago when terrorists flew planes into the World Trade Center and Pentagon and crashed a fourth into the countryside of Pennsylvania after passengers fought back.

Mr. Trump was just a few miles away from the trade center at the time and gave an interview that day saying he could see an explosion from his window. He said that one of his buildings had been the second largest in New York before the towers fell. “Now, it’s the tallest,” he said, which actually was not true.

His other stories of that period have been factually challenged as well. He has repeatedly claimed to have gone to the attack site with a large crew of construction workers to help, an assertion that has been questioned just as repeatedly. In a speech on Tuesday, Mr. Trump even said that two firefighters physically lifted him to evacuate from an unstable nearby building, a claim for which there is no evidence. And he has spread the debunked legend that “thousands and thousands” of Muslims in New Jersey cheered as the towers collapsed.

Mr. Trump’s decision to skip Friday’s ceremony in New York has raised eyebrows. Several people close to the situation told The New York Times that one reason Mr. Trump decided not to go to ground zero was because by tradition no speeches are given there on the anniversary and he wanted to speak. Mr. Trump has angrily denied this. Asked why he was not going to New York, he said, “because I’m going to the Pentagon.”

He did not explain why he could not go to New York as well as the Pentagon nor would the White House when asked. On other big anniversaries, Mr. Bush (on the first and fifth), Mr. Obama (on the 10th) and Mr. Biden (on the 20th) each visited all three attack sites on the same day. Mr. Trump plans to leave on Friday after the Pentagon event for a weekend at his golf club in Doonbeg, Ireland, and one person briefed on the matter previously told The Times it would be easier for him to fly out of Joint Base Andrews outside Washington than from a commercial airport in New York.

Each of the presidents who will be in New York on Friday confronted terrorism while in office. Mr. Clinton was the first to encounter and pursue Al Qaeda, which bombed U.S. embassies in Africa in 1998. Mr. Bush found his presidency completely transformed on Sept. 11 and kicked off wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. Mr. Obama ordered the commando raid that resulted in the killing of bin Laden, only to have the Islamic State emerge in his second term.

Mr. Biden as a senator and vice president helped shape post-Sept. 11 policy. Then as president, he pulled American forces from Afghanistan two decades after they arrived in the aftermath of the attacks on the United States, a withdrawal negotiated by Mr. Trump in his first term. The pullout allowed the Taliban to sweep back to power, a dark coda to a 20-year failed war, though Mr. Biden did succeed in killing bin Laden’s deputy Ayman al-Zawahri with a drone strike in Kabul.

Mr. Trump was a private citizen through much of this until he ran for president in 2016 and vowed a tougher approach to terrorism. Unlike Mr. Bush, who emphasized that the United States was not at war with Islam and made a point of visiting a mosque shortly after Sept. 11, Mr. Trump called for “a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States” and promised to bring back waterboarding prisoners to obtain intelligence because “torture works.”

He was tested just days after taking office in 2017 when he was asked to authorize a raid in Yemen that cost the life of a Navy Seal, a moment that advisers said shook him. He later found more confidence as he announced the killing of Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, the Islamic State leader, in 2019 and a couple of months later ordered the assassination of Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani, the Iranian security and intelligence commander who organized terrorist attacks on American troops in Iraq.

Mr. Hoffman, the terrorism scholar, said both of those operations were major victories for Mr. Trump and “extremely significant.” He also said Mr. Trump “gets the highest marks of any president” for his focus on winning freedom for hostages held overseas, including by terrorist groups.

At the same time, he added, “the deprioritization of terrorism” more broadly, while “it could have been inevitable under another presidency,” has its potential perils. “All of those things, have they left us weaker?” he asked. “Only time will tell.”

item.title: Sam Bankman-Fried Asks Supreme Court to Review Fraud Conviction
item.description:
Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of the once-powerful FTX cryptocurrency exchange, asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to overturn his conviction.

Mr. Bankman-Fried is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence after a jury convicted the crypto entrepreneur of fraud, conspiracy and money laundering in 2023. Federal prosecutors had accused him of running one of the largest financial frauds in history, stealing billions of dollars from FTX customers while holding himself out as a responsible philanthropist.

It is not clear whether the justices will agree to take up Mr. Bankman-Fried’s case. They typically receive thousands of such requests each year, and agree to hear arguments in about 60 cases.

Mr. Bankman-Fried founded FTX in 2019 and quickly grew it into one of the largest crypto exchanges in the world, a move that brought him wealth and fame and made him one of the world’s youngest billionaires. He became a top Democratic donor and cultivated relationships with celebrities and business leaders.

His empire collapsed in stunning fashion in 2022, after a run on deposits forced the firm to file for bankruptcy, prompting criminal investigations. He was arrested later that year in the Bahamas, where he had been living, before being extradited to the U.S. to face trial.

Mr. Bankman-Fried, who has maintained his innocence, was convicted after a monthlong federal jury trial. He appealed, but his conviction was upheld in June by a three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.

In a petition to the justices, lawyers for Mr. Bankman-Fried asserted that review by the Supreme Court was “urgently necessary,” arguing that Mr. Bankman-Fried should have been allowed to present evidence that none of FTX’s customers lost money as a result of his actions. The Times reviewed a copy of the petition.

They argued that the trial court also erred by blocking Mr. Bankman-Fried from presenting evidence of his claims that “there were always more than enough assets available to repay customers (as they now have been repaid, with substantial interest).”

Under a plan filed in federal bankruptcy court, virtually all of FTX’s creditors, including the investors who used the crypto exchange for buying and selling cryptocurrencies, were promised cash payments, including interest, to recover all of the money they lost.

Federal prosecutors have argued that FTX’s customers were defrauded through Mr. Bankman-Fried’s handling of their money, including “misappropriating billions of dollars of those customers’ funds,” regardless whether those customers were ultimately able to recover their money.

Lawyers for Mr. Bankman-Fried also challenged the trial court’s order that he forfeit about $11 billion in assets. They argued it was a “crushing fine” that collided with the Eighth Amendment’s protection against excessive fines.

Separately, Mr. Bankman-Fried has applied for a pardon from President Trump, according to online records. The Office of the Pardon Attorney, a division of the Justice Department, has listed Mr. Bankman-Fried’s request for a “pardon after completion of sentence” as “pending.”

item.title: While Trump Goes Big in Dallas, Collins Goes Small in Maine to Save Her Seat
item.description:
Hours before many of her Republican colleagues and those seeking to join their ranks convened in a hulking Dallas arena for a two-day political rally headlined by President Trump, Senator Susan Collins stood in a 10,000-square-foot recreation center in central Maine on Wednesday and examined the ceiling.

Instead of the balloons and klieg lights that adorned the rafters hundreds of miles to the south at Mr. Trump’s extravagant midterm convention, Ms. Collins looked up and saw fluorescent bulbs and water stains that prompted her to ask the town’s manager if the building had a leaky roof.

“We did,” the manager, Dylan Lajoie, told her. But, he said, because of a $935,000 grant Ms. Collins had secured in a federal spending bill for the town of Newport, it had been possible to renovate and “refresh” the facility.

This is how Ms. Collins, at 73 seeking her sixth term in the Senate, is working to defend her job in a state that Mr. Trump lost, at a time when Republicans face strong political headwinds because of his flagging approval ratings.

To win re-election in November, Ms. Collins, a moderate who has been critical of the president and opposed some elements of his agenda, is deploying the same strategy that has kept her in the Senate for decades. She is keeping her distance from Mr. Trump and her party’s national brand and message, and instead highlighting local issues and how she has used her position in Washington, including as the chairwoman of the powerful Appropriations Committee, to deliver for her tiny state.

It is a matter of political survival for Ms. Collins, who is viewed as the most vulnerable Republican incumbent and is facing harsh criticism from Democrats who accuse her of failing to stand up to Mr. Trump even as she often expresses grave concern about his policies and actions.

Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, a former State Senate president, has tried to make the election a referendum on the president and tag Ms. Collins as “a puppet” for him. He has pointed to her voting record as he works to persuade moderate and independent voters who have backed her in the past that she has not done enough to thwart Mr. Trump’s agenda.

With control of the Senate at stake, Ms. Collins must now confront whether her longstanding relationship with Maine voters can overcome an increasingly partisan political environment.

“Legitimate question,” Ms. Collins said in an interview Wednesday afternoon outside the recreation center, where contractors were excavating a lot for a new athletic field. “There’s no doubt that our politics are far more polarized than they used to be. But Maine people are practical, and they want results. They don’t want someone who’s just going to rant and rave and be hyperpartisan.”

Back in Dallas, Mr. Trump and Republicans from across the country were making the opposite case at their midterm political convention, which appeared geared toward animating the president’s right-wing base.

During their speeches, Republicans repeatedly attacked Democrats, characterizing them as overly left-wing and bent on destroying the country. Mr. Trump dismissed concerns about the high cost of living, defended unpopular trade policies, promised a payout to Americans if the G.O.P. won and urged his supporters to act as if they were voting for him.

“Please pretend that I am running,” Mr. Trump told Americans across the country.

Ms. Collins — who told reporters on Thursday that she “did not get a chance” to watch Mr. Trump’s speech and was “not familiar” with his proposed checks to Americans — would perhaps rather that Maine residents pretended he wasn’t.

Mr. Trump lost Maine in the past three presidential elections, and many of his policies are felt acutely here. With winter approaching, residents are concerned about the rise in fuel and heating oil prices driven by wars in Iran and Ukraine. The escalating trade war with Canada has worried businesses that are reliant on the country, which Maine borders, as a trading partner.

Ms. Collins has repeatedly objected to Mr. Trump’s tariffs on Canada, and she has tried to distance herself from them. On Thursday morning, she stood with the owners of a sand and gravel business in Naples, Maine, and said that she had pushed the White House to remove tariffs on road salt and cement.

“I’ve urged the administration to get back to the table and negotiate with Canada,” she said.

Yet even as she criticized his policies, Ms. Collins avoided mentioning Mr. Trump by name, sticking instead to her own work and the problems facing her constituents. (Like many other politically vulnerable Republicans, she skipped the Dallas convention, aides said, in line with her longstanding policy of forgoing such party gatherings whenever she is up for re-election.)

During Wednesday’s bus tour, Ms. Collins talked about legislation that helped small businesses while she shopped at an outdoor sporting goods store. At a credit union, she spoke to workers about a law she sponsored to protect older Americans from predatory financial scams. She stopped at Newport’s fire station and talked to the fire chief and a captain about directing federal funds to firefighters in the state.

Still, Ms. Collins could not escape the shadow of Mr. Trump’s policies. The Newport Fire Department is across the street from a building that state lawmakers said would be turned into a federal immigration facility.

Ms. Collins told a local reporter that she had not been aware of that plan, and she sought to highlight her role in allocating funding for body-worn cameras. But Democrats have criticized Ms. Collins for not doing enough to curb the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, particularly a fatal shooting by an ICE agent in the state earlier this year.

Mr. Jackson has not had much time to introduce himself to voters. A CNN poll released on Wednesday, during Ms. Collins’s bus tour, showed a close race but also found that a significant chunk of likely voters did not yet have a clear impression of Mr. Jackson.

So far, however, he has centered his campaign largely on trying to turn Ms. Collins’s long experience into a liability.

“It’s never been more important to elect a U.S. senator that will stand up to him,” Mr. Jackson said on Wednesday at an event with a teachers union, referring to Mr. Trump. “I don’t have to tell you that Susan Collins won’t do that. You just have to look at her record.”

Ms. Collins is banking on her constituents choosing the candidate they know, particularly after her initial opponent, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race in July after a sexual assault allegation and was replaced by Mr. Jackson.

Most of her stops were sparsely attended, with the senator accompanied by her staff and met by volunteers and supporters who were trailing the bus through town.

Still, when she stopped for chicken tenders and fries at Sawyer’s Dairy Bar in Newport, Ms. Collins, a longtime political fixture in the state, was stopped repeatedly by customers who recognized her and asked for photos.

Elizabeth Hook, 83, said that she had previously met Ms. Collins when the apparel company where she worked at the time opened a factory in Maine. A Republican who has at times crossed party lines to vote for Democrats, Ms. Hook said that she would be sticking with Ms. Collins this year. She commended the senator for continuing to work across the aisle.

“You know, it’s not a war between Republicans and Democrats, but for God’s sakes, we’ve got to get along,” Ms. Hook said. “We’ve got to compromise. She has a good head on her shoulders, and I can’t throw that away for a fly-by-night.”

item.title: Some in G.O.P. Balk at Trump’s $5,000 Offer: ‘We’re $40 Trillion in Debt’
item.description:
Republicans spent the first five hours of their midterm convention in Dallas warning about socialism on Wednesday before President Trump surprised many of them with an audacious trillion-dollar proposal to redistribute wealth.

Mr. Trump’s call to send $5,000 to every adult American — but only if his party wins in November — was quickly denounced by Democrats, who accused him of trying to buy people’s votes. But it also was panned by some Republican fiscal hawks as a socialist-style giveaway and gimmick that could have harmful economic repercussions.

“We’re $40 trillion in debt,” said Representative Ralph Norman, Republican of South Carolina and the vice chairman of the House Freedom Caucus, who called the idea “far-fetched” in an interview. “To make that dependent on keeping the House, I think is problematic and I don’t know where the money comes from.”

Joe Lonsdale, a co-founder of Palantir and a major Republican donor who was a co-host of a Wednesday night party at the Dallas convention with one of Mr. Trump’s sons, Donald Trump Jr., was unimpressed by the proposal.

“For the record, I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this admin, but am strongly against bread and circus bribes,” he wrote on X when his event, billed as The Great American Midterm Party, was scheduled to be underway.

Mr. Trump’s elect-us-we-pay-you plan dismayed a number of Republicans who were not close to the president.

Marc Short, who served as the White House legislative affairs director in Mr. Trump’s first term and as former Vice President Mike Pence’s chief of staff, called the $5,000 proposal the latest in “a series of policy adjustments that blur the line between us and democratic socialists.”

Mr. Short ticked through a list that included the government taking a stake in private enterprises, implementing price controls, capping credit card fees and a labor-friendly trade agenda.

“He understands the marketing. He understands the moment. I don’t think he prioritizes the economics,” Mr. Short said. “Basically, it’s a redistribution of wealth.”

The potential payments, which were estimated to cost roughly $1.3 trillion, could complicate a number of the administration’s pressing economic goals. With Mr. Trump silent on how he would be pay for the proposal, it threatened to add to a national debt that has exceeded $40 trillion, causing jitters in the bond market that the Trump administration has been struggling to contain.

And at a moment when voters are blaming the Trump administration for not doing enough to tame rising costs, the trillion-dollar payment could act much like the Biden-era stimulus measures that Mr. Trump and other Republicans blamed for spiraling inflation. On Thursday, the European Central Bank raised interest rates to the highest level in a year in an effort to tame inflation, blaming the war in Iran for worsening inflation pressure. Federal Reserve officials will consider raising rates next week.

Representative Chip Roy, a Texas Republican and a prominent fiscal hawk, said in a text message that “A trillion and a half dollars of inflationary deficit spending is not my preferred focus, to say the least.”

Of course, for the last decade, Mr. Trump has defined Republican economic policy and discarded much of the party’s longstanding economic goals. Largely gone are concerns about debts and deficits and strict adherence to free-market and free-trade principles.

Asked by Laura Ingraham during a Fox News interview on Thursday, “if you have the money, why not give it now,” Mr. Trump blamed Democrats, even though Republicans control both chambers of Congress, and went on to talk about tariffs.

It was not immediately clear whether the Republicans who control Congress had any appetite to push for the measure.

Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the Republican majority leader, said on Fox News on Thursday that it was a “good question” whether there would be votes for such a package. “We will cross that bridge when we come to it,” Mr. Thune said.

Speaker Mike Johnson has not commented publicly.

Mr. Trump has a long history of making big promises he has failed to win support for. Earlier this term he promised a DOGE dividend paid for with money Elon Musk’s team cut from the federal budget and a “tariff refund” funded with money the government was collecting in import taxes. Neither happened.

Still, the $5,000 offer tied to the midterms proved Mr. Trump still has the ability to shock.

“The policy community on all sides is aghast,” said Maya MacGuineas, the president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, who was in bed reading a book Wednesday night when she received a flurry of text messages about what Mr. Trump had proposed.

Still she did not discount the possibility of Republicans, should they win the midterms, finding a way to legislate Mr. Trump’s proposal into reality.

“Trump has an incredible power over his party to create support where there wouldn’t have been otherwise,” she said. “It’s really hard to say no to giveaways.”

At least some Republicans were enthusiastic about the proposal. Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio wrote that he would prepare legislation “so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately.”

But a parade of Republicans from the party’s diminished old guard registered their disapproval online. Former Gov. Asa Hutchison of Arkansas warned about the national debt and said that Republicans “should be the adults in the room” and reject Mr. Trump’s proposal. Former Representative Justin Amash of Michigan called it a “ridiculous, unrealizable bribe.” And The National Review condemned the proposal under a headline: “Trump Breaks Glass, Joins Socialists, Embraces Bribery.”

The White House did not respond to requests for more details about the president’s plan or questions about criticisms of his proposal.

The policy-minded defense of Mr. Trump’s proposal was left to allies who were intellectually versatile.

Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, appearing on Fox News right after Mr. Trump finished speaking, called $5,000 a “real incentive” even as he tried to attack the other party.

“The Democrats love offering free money,” Mr. Cruz said, just after Mr. Trump’s offer of free money. He went on to attempt to erect some conservative intellectual scaffolding around Mr. Trump’s thin giveaway proposal.

“One way to conceive this that is also an incentive for work is that it’s a tax rebate,” he said. I’d like to see as many incentives as possible for work.”

Mr. Trump did not frame the $5,000 as a tax rebate.

Vice President JD Vance was asked about the proposal on the same network by the hosts Bret Baier and Sean Hannity.

“You guys don’t need it,” Mr. Vance said. “This is for the American middle class.”

That is not how Mr. Trump described it, either.

He said in his convention address that if Republicans hold on to power in Congress: “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”

item.title: Outside, Tough Midterms Loomed. Inside, It Was ‘Trump-a-palooza.’
item.description:
President Trump’s celebration of self kicked off this week in Dallas with the dazzle that he demands: a tenor garbed in an amethyst velvet smoking jacket belting out “America the Beautiful.”

The same tenor, Christopher Macchio, had sung at Mr. Trump’s last two Republican National Conventions. Perhaps recreating the scene could conjure the political magic of elections past.

Conjuring magic appeared to be a central purpose of this rare midterm gathering, with the president boasting of his accomplishments, predicting Republican victories and all but ignoring the daunting political landscape outside the arena.

The fall midterm elections have not looked promising for months. Mr. Trump’s popularity has dropped drastically, undone by an affordability crisis prompted by some of his biggest policies, including tariffs and the war in Iran. He glossed over those issues, insisting the war would end soon and gas prices would go down. It wasn’t clear how much that would help Republicans actually running.

The convention, at the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas, featured some of the usual elements of presidential nominating conventions, with an inescapable Texas flair: Sequined cowboy hats. A peak heat index on Wednesday of around 102. A lineup of Republican speakers onstage and Republican faithful in the seats.

The gathering also mimicked a presidential convention by focusing almost exclusively on Mr. Trump — and not the men and women fighting to retain Republican control of Congress. The credentials to get in displayed Mr. Trump’s picture. Enlarged photos decked the corridors showing Mr. Trump from all angles, including one of his bandaged ear after a 2024 assassination attempt. Asked about whom they were excited to see, attendees did not pretend for a moment that the bash was about anyone other than the man whose name will not be on the November ballot.

“Obviously, President Trump,” said Alexandria Hughes of the U.S. Virgin Islands, who has attended Republican conventions for decades, as she clutched her 2-year-old Maltese service dog, Lucia Christabella. “Because he’s always so much fun.”

The president acknowledged in a nearly two-hour stemwinder on Wednesday night that few presidents see their parties do well in the midterms, though he posited that “nobody quite knows why.”

“It’s something deep down and psychological,” he mused. Then, he added: “We have to change that.”

Ergo, “Trump-a-palooza” in Dallas. Mr. Trump boasted about his policies, convinced that the strategy for victory is to make the midterms a referendum on his presidency. “TRUMP WAS RIGHT ABOUT EVERYTHING!” read red baseball hats in the style of MAGA.

Republican candidates in competitive House and Senate races, while eager to praise the president, were also careful to shy away from more prickly specifics on unpopular issues.

“You’ve always got to be worried — they’re elections, not coronations,” said Bill Helmich, the executive director of the Republican Party of Florida, which had distributed bespoke cowboy belt buckles for the event. “But President Trump is our best messenger.”

For a president who places a high value on slick productions, the convention, thrown together with much less notice than one in the summer before a presidential election, was a little rough around the edges. The enlarged Trump posters in the arena were a little blurry. Early on in Wednesday’s program, the still-thin crowd had to be coached to cheer.

And despite Mr. Trump’s claims to the contrary, some seats were empty, even during his address. (“If you don’t mind,” he told attendees, preemptively criticizing news reports about the crowd size, “don’t anybody go to the bathroom.”) Elsewhere, millions of voters were surely watching the N.F.L. season opener, a Super Bowl rematch between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots, rather than political speeches.

The convention did bring together candidates, operatives and some donors, who met behind closed doors and held court at the bar in several luxe hotels — the Ritz, the W, the Joule — to discuss matters such as campaign strategy and spending. The Republican National Committee held its summer meeting at the Hilton Anatole, with massive elephant statues in the lobby that were procured ahead of the 1984 Republican convention in Dallas. Among the breakfast buffet offerings were eggs Benedict, Liège-style waffles and Belgian chocolate fondue.

Back at the arena, Derek Turbide, 25, the executive director of the North Dakota Republican Party, said the event felt different from the presidential nominating convention in 2024 because there were fewer politicians and more “everyday Americans.”

Mr. Turbide came to Dallas with 34 other North Dakotans. Half of them were donors who paid between $3,500 and $1,250 to be in the arena, he said, and half were Republicans from the state who “don’t usually get to attend the big events.”

“Even little North Dakotans can make it to the front at R.N.C. ’26,” he said. A significant subset of seats at the front of the arena were reserved for nonpolitical figures, including a devoted group of rally-goers known as “front row Joes.”

On Wednesday afternoon, as speakers began to take the stage, an aide approached Mr. Turbide with four extra tickets to disperse to North Dakotans to fill the section.

“Where do they go?” Mr. Turbide asked.

“There’s still open seating,” the aide said. “Up in the front.”

Emily Davies contributed reporting from Dallas.

item.title: Trump Loyalist Steps Down From ‘Grand Conspiracy’ Case
item.description:
A loyalist prosecutor handpicked by the Justice Department to lead a contentious conspiracy investigation into several of President Trump’s political opponents abruptly quit his job on Thursday, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The prosecutor, Joseph diGenova, had been in charge of what Mr. Trump’s allies have often referred to as the “grand conspiracy,” a sprawling inquiry based in the U.S. attorney’s office in South Florida that has sought to implicate federal officials who have investigated Mr. Trump in a single plot to deprive him of his rights.

Mr. diGenova’s resignation was the latest setback in the case that began last year and has dragged on for months. Even though members of his team have issued numerous grand jury subpoenas to federal law enforcement and intelligence officials who have sought over the past decade to hold Mr. Trump accountable in a series of criminal inquiries, Mr. diGenova had yet to obtain an indictment.

“It was an honor and privilege to serve the president and the department,” Mr. DiGenova told CNN and CBS during phone interviews on Thursday.

A spokeswoman for the U.S. attorney’s office did not respond to a message seeking comment.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly put pressure on prosecutors to bring criminal charges against his opponents, calling them out in private meetings and in social media posts. He has also expressed displeasure about the slow pace of the retributive investigations he has helped to set in motion.

But time and again, Mr. Trump’s desire for vengeance and his willingness to break through the walls of independence that have traditionally separated the White House and the Justice Department have resulted in failure. Judges and grand juries have repeatedly stymied his attempts to strong arm prosecutors into bringing charges.

Sometimes, as in the case of Mr. diGenova, the prosecutors themselves have effectively reminded him that it is no simple matter to file indictments against people without real evidence or viable legal reasoning.

With his move, Mr. diGenova became the second prosecutor who has either resigned or been removed from the grand conspiracy case. The prosecutor in charge of an early phase of the investigation was forced to leave in the spring after telling her superiors that there was not sufficient evidence to bring charges against one of its first targets, John O. Brennan, a former C.I.A. director who provoked Mr. Trump’s ire by helping to assemble an intelligence assessment that determined that Russia had sought to interfere in the 2016 presidential campaign.

The grand conspiracy inquiry has long been the most fevered of the many revenge investigations that Mr. Trump has demanded the Justice Department undertake. It has involved prosecutors seeking to link disparate criminal inquiries into the president — including the Russia investigation and a separate investigation into Mr. Trump’s mishandling of classified documents — as an overarching, multiyear scheme to damage his political prospects.

From the outset, Mr. diGenova faced an uphill battle in seeking to prove the basic theory of his case: that the various inquiries into Mr. Trump — conducted by different prosecutors and spanning nearly a decade — could be reasonably tied together in a single conspiracy. Those hurdles have led several current and former prosecutors in the office in southern Florida to wonder whether the investigation was largely a show put on to placate Mr. Trump.

Mr. diGenova, a former U.S. attorney from the Reagan era who had not worked as a prosecutor in nearly 40 years, took control of the case in April after his predecessor, Maria Medetis Long, was kicked off the investigation. At 81, he was an unusual choice to oversee an inquiry involving multiple targets that quickly grew to include at least a dozen prosecutors, including his wife, Victoria Toensing.

Moreover, Mr. diGenova was a longtime ally of Mr. Trump’s who had publicly claimed that the Russia investigation was a plot by law enforcement to frame him and keep him out of the White House. Mr. diGenova also worked as a lawyer for Mr. Trump’s 2020 campaign, supporting his false assertions that the election that year had been rigged against him.

While Mr. Brennan was the initial focus of the inquiry, it has also involved an effort to implicate James B. Comey, the former F.B.I. director, who has already been charged in a separate case in North Carolina. Late last month, Mr. diGenova’s office issued a subpoena demanding testimony from one of Mr. Comey’s close confidants.

item.title: Justice Dept. Opens Inquiry Into Clippers’ Dealings With Star Player
item.description:
Federal prosecutors have opened a criminal investigation into allegations that the Los Angeles Clippers helped arrange secret sponsorship contracts for the star player Kawhi Leonard that circumvented the salary cap, according to people briefed on the matter.

The investigation is in its earliest stages and is being conducted by the U.S. attorney’s office in Brooklyn, which has a long history of investigating the N.B.A. and professional sports, according to two of the people.

The authorities began scrutinizing the matter before the N.B.A. leveled a series of severe punishments last week against the Clippers, its owner and two top executives after a law firm working for the N.B.A. and its commissioner, Adam Silver, concluded that the team had engaged in a wide-ranging effort to break its rules.

The inquiry’s scope, targets and the possible crimes being examined were unclear. But prosecutors have issued at least one subpoena as part of the investigation, according to the two people.

John Marzulli, a spokesman for the U.S. attorney’s office, declined to comment. Spokesmen for the Clippers and the N.B.A. did not respond to messages seeking comment on whether they are cooperating with the investigation or if they received a subpoena.

Among the matters likely under scrutiny are a series of secret endorsement deals that Mr. Leonard signed, and whether Steve Ballmer, the team’s owner, and other executives helped facilitate them as a way of compensating him at a level that exceeded the N.B.A.’s salary cap.

The very existence of the investigation adds a complex dynamic for the parties involved, including the Clippers, Mr. Leonard and the team’s sponsors. Already, they are facing the fallout from the league’s punishments and a scathing report by a white-shoe law firm on the allegations.

The Clippers and Mr. Ballmer are still trying to figure out how to respond to the punishments from the N.B.A. Among the potential moves they are considering is whether to bring a lawsuit against the league, asking a judge to issue a restraining order, the two people said.

The people briefed on the matter cautioned that it was uncertain whether the investigation would lead to criminal charges, or even result in evidence being presented to a grand jury. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a continuing investigation.

For nearly two decades, the U.S. attorney’s office in Brooklyn has brought cases that focused on integrity in professional sports.

In 2007, the office and the F.B.I. brought a case against an N.B.A. referee who admitted to gambling on games that he officiated. Over the past two years, prosecutors in the office, the Eastern District of New York, have charged eight current and former professional athletes in cases involving illegal gambling. Among the defendants have been the Hall of Fame N.B.A. guard Chauncey Billups and the star Major League Baseball closer Emmanuel Clase, both of whom have pleaded not guilty.

In 2015, Brooklyn federal prosecutors charged dozens of defendants in a case targeting widespread institutional corruption in FIFA, the governing body of global soccer. The case uncovered a scheme in which sports marketing executives paid $150 million in bribes to soccer officials in exchange for the lucrative broadcast rights to tournaments.

The journalist Pablo Torre first raised questions about the Clippers’ dealings with Mr. Leonard on his podcast, “Pablo Torre Finds Out,” in September 2025. In response, the N.B.A. began an investigation, hiring the law firm of Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation. (“Pablo Torre Finds Out” is an independently produced show licensed by The Athletic, which is owned by The New York Times.)

Under its salary cap, the N.B.A. limits how much a team can spend on its players, in part as a way to promote competition. In July 2019, Mr. Leonard signed a three-year contract worth more than $100 million. But according to the report by Wachtell, Mr. Leonard, through his uncle, Dennis Robertson, pressured the Clippers into providing endorsement deals that were worth tens of millions of dollars more, defying N.B.A. rules.

The endorsements were never announced publicly, and Mr. Leonard did no public endorsement work for the companies. One of the agreements that drew particular attention was a $28 million deal with Aspiration Partners, a sustainability company that is now bankrupt. The company had also signed a series of deals with the Clippers and Mr. Ballmer.

The law firm released its findings into the Clippers’ dealings early this month saying that the Clippers had violated the N.B.A.’s salary cap rules by “affirmatively initiating off-court income opportunities between Mr. Leonard and four different companies.”

The N.B.A. said it had found “a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations by the Clippers organization” and issued one of the harshest penalties in its history. It stripped the Clippers of five future draft picks, a move that heavily restricts the team’s ability to improve for years to come. Mr. Leonard was ordered to pay $700,000 in restitution to the N.B.A., while the Clippers were docked $30 million and Mr. Ballmer was suspended from the league for one year.

Two other Clippers executives involved were suspended, as was Mr. Leonard’s uncle, Mr. Robertson.

In response to the N.B.A.’s action, Mr. Leonard said in a statement that he had accepted “responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle.”

The Clippers strenuously pushed back on the N.B.A. and Mr. Silver.

“We vehemently reject the N.B.A.’s findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence,” the Clippers said in a statement. “What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly.”

The Justice Department is the second arm of the government to look into what happened between the Clippers and Mr. Leonard.

Daktronics, a company that manufactures jumbo screens in arenas and had one of the sponsorship deals with Mr. Leonard that the N.B.A. singled out in its report, acknowledged to investors in early September that the Securities and Exchange Commission had sought information from it and Mr. Leonard.

The company said it was cooperating with that inquiry.

item.title: No Trump Bump for Fox News’s Coverage of President’s Dallas Speech
item.description:
President Trump has long been a marquee draw on television, with Fox News viewers in particular often showing up in droves to watch his fiery and grievance-filled speeches.

But the president’s 105-minute stemwinder on Wednesday in Dallas, at an unusual midterm convention meant to stoke Republican enthusiasm before November, did not appear to generate the usual Trump Bump.

An average of 2.5 million people tuned in to watch Mr. Trump between 9 and 11 p.m. Eastern on Fox News, one of the few major TV networks that aired his remarks in full. It was more or less an average prime-time audience for Fox News, based on the most recent quarterly statistics.

The Fox News audience also dipped below the usual viewership for “Hannity” and “Gutfeld!,” the programs that regularly air during that time slot, according to preliminary figures from Nielsen.

Mr. Trump had faced some stiff competition: the first game of the National Football League season, which aired against his speech on NBC. Last year, more than 20 million people watched the opener. NBC said that Nielsen ratings for Wednesday’s telecast, a Super Bowl rematch between the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks, would not be available until next week.

Mr. Trump’s speech was also available to watch on countless streaming services and digital outlets, where many Americans now consume their news. Viewership figures for those digital platforms are difficult to accurately track.

Traditional TV viewers who wanted to watch Mr. Trump on Wednesday had fewer options to follow along live. ABC, CBS and NBC did not pre-empt weeknight programming for Mr. Trump. CNN aired less than 15 minutes of his remarks, while MS NOW occasionally ran a split screen. C-SPAN took the speech in full, but Nielsen does not measure its viewership.

Mr. Trump was expected to speak again in Dallas on Thursday. Another N.F.L. game will be streaming on Netflix.

item.title: What to Know About Missouri’s High-Stakes Election Map Battle
item.description:
Missouri’s congressional map has been the subject of bitter court fights since Republican legislators redrew the lines last year to boost their party’s odds in the midterm elections.

A dizzying volley of court rulings in recent days has created widespread confusion about which boundaries will be in effect in November and about how long any single decision on the matter might hold.

Three courts weighed in on the issue on Thursday, leaving the state of play for the general election in November somewhat clearer and renewing Democrats’ hope of holding a seat that could help determine control of Congress.

Here’s what to know about how we got here and what might happen next:

For the second time in a week, the Supreme Court issued a decision that prevented Missouri from using the new map.

The latest order left in place a Missouri Supreme Court ruling that instructed election officials to use the lines that had been in force since 2022 this November. The primary election last month was held using the redrawn boundaries.

Missouri’s top election official, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, said he would comply with the order.

The court’s order and Mr. Hoskins’s pledge to abide by it represented a significant win for Democrats and a blow to the Republicans who redrew the lines at President Trump’s request.

If no additional courts intervene, Democrats would be favored to retain a Kansas City-area House seat that Republicans had hoped to flip. The state’s U.S. House delegation is likely to continue to include six Republicans and two Democrats.

But even after what might have appeared to be decisive rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court, more court fights seem likely.

On Thursday, after the U.S. Supreme Court announced its decision, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit scheduled oral arguments for next week in a case filed by a Republican congressman and a Republican candidate for Congress who want the redrawn lines to be used in the general election. But any further ruling in that case would not take effect without additional action from the U.S. Supreme Court.

There is little precedent for holding a general election with different district lines from those used in a primary, and no court has specified how Missouri’s nominees should be selected. It seems likeliest that the candidates who won their primaries under the redrawn map would remain the nominees in the same-numbered districts on the old map.

Even as the secretary of state’s office instructed county election officials on Thursday to prepare for the November election using the older lines, Republicans signaled that they would not drop the issue.

“I look forward to the Eighth Circuit’s consideration of the merits of the Missouri First Map and remain confident in the legal process moving forward,” Gov. Mike Kehoe said on Thursday, referring to the redrawn map.

Missouri was one of the first states to join Mr. Trump’s redistricting push last year. The new map sliced the core of Kansas City, Missouri’s largest city, into several districts, placing Democratic-leaning urban voters in squiggly-lined districts that stretched well into the state’s conservative countryside.

The new map would likely have ended the congressional career of Representative Emanuel Cleaver, an 11-term Democrat from Kansas City who was also the city’s first Black mayor, and delivered his seat to a Republican. In a close election nationally, that seat could help swing partisan control of Congress. Mr. Cleaver is seeking re-election.

Even if the older lines are used in November, the redrawn boundaries could still eventually take effect. Because hundreds of thousands of Missourians signed petitions seeking a statewide vote on the new map, the State Supreme Court said the new lines would be suspended until voters weighed in. That vote will take place in November.

Missouri’s highest court found that Mr. Hoskins had been in civil contempt for not moving quickly enough to implement its order to return to the older map. But because Mr. Hoskins reversed course on Thursday, the court said he was no longer in contempt and took no further action against him.

Until the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision on Thursday, Mr. Hoskins had said he planned to follow a federal district judge’s order to use the new map instead of the unanimous State Supreme Court order to return to the older lines. Five of the seven Missouri Supreme Court judges were appointed by Republican governors.

In a hearing on Thursday that started just minutes after the U.S. Supreme Court issued its order, many of the Missouri judges were visibly frustrated as a lawyer for Mr. Hoskins said the state was “evaluating next steps” and did not promise to return to the older lines.

“We’re in a precarious situation,” Chief Justice W. Brent Powell said, adding that he was trying to “save some of these elections so that they are valid” and so that Missouri’s next congressional delegation could be seated.

Ann E. Marimow and Bernard Mokam contributed reporting.

item.title: Fears of a Democratic Wave Push Texas to Center Stage at G.O.P. Convention
item.description:
The Republicans selected Dallas for their unusual midterm gathering in large part out of convenience. It’s a big city accustomed to big conventions, in a Republican-friendly state where they could confidently pull off a relatively last-minute event of the scope desired by President Trump, party officials said.

But Texas is not just the incidental backdrop for an event aimed at a national television audience; it took center stage for much of the convention. The focus was a sign of the growing concern among Republicans that a wave of Democratic enthusiasm could even breach Texas’s red wall in November.

Much of the attention was on Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general and nominee for U.S. Senate, who was trailing James Talarico, his Democratic opponent, in many polls. President Trump vowed in his speech on Wednesday to come back to Texas “twice or three times” to support Mr. Paxton, while also acknowledging the candidate did not always impress.

“He may not dress right,” the president said. “He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.”

There were also speeches from three congressional candidates who are running in districts specifically designed by the Texas legislature last year to favor a Republican. Each is facing a tough election fight despite the new lines.

One of them, Tano Tijerina, who is trying to oust Representative Henry Cuellar, a Democrat in South Texas, delivered a rousing, red-meat speech, his eyes shadowed by a large cowboy hat. Loud cheers erupted as he described himself as “beef-eating, truck-driving, gunslinging,” prompting him to stop midsentence and point to the sky.

There were backdrops of West Texas on the screen and more cowboy hats than usual in the arena, which usually hosts the Dallas Mavericks of the N.B.A. and the Dallas Stars of the N.H.L. Of the speeches reserved for “everyday Americans,” several came from Texans who spoke of their experience on the Mexican border or resisting gender-transition care in Texas hospitals.

Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, who is running for a fourth term, described Texas as the first bulwark against a liberal invasion of communists and socialists, a frequent refrain among speakers throughout the convention. A loss in Texas, he warned, would cascade across the country.

“In Texas, we have a saying: We have to get it right because there’s not another Texas to move to in November,” Mr. Patrick said on Thursday. “We have to get it right because there’s not another America to move to.”

And Senator Ted Cruz, who is not on the ballot in November, put the spotlight on an issue that has been a focus of Texas Republicans this election season: Islam.

State leaders have taken steps over the last year to curtail the activities of Muslim organizations. In a dark speech on Thursday that assailed Muslim Democrats and reflected a growing tolerance for Islamophobia among some party officials, Mr. Cruz falsely portrayed such officials as seeking to impose strict Islamic religious rules.

“Shariah law has no place in America,” Mr. Cruz said, drawing huge applause from the audience on Thursday. “We need to stand together and stop it now.”

But Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the U.S. House, said the party should not be too worried about losing in Texas, even in Mr. Paxton’s race with Mr. Talarico.

“We’ll be fine,” he said as he walked through the convention on Wednesday. “Texas has a cyclical pattern of the bright, articulate new hope, who raises an amazing amount of money. And then Texans realize, ‘Why, he’s a Democrat!’”

item.title: Hawaii Governor Asks Trump for Help as State Copes With Hurricane’s Damage
item.description:
As Hawaii residents continue to cope with the aftermath of two rare hurricanes in recent weeks, the state’s governor has asked President Trump for help.

Thousands of people in the state remained without power on Thursday. Long lines at gas stations, damaged roads and downed power lines were reported on Kauai, the island of about 73,000 people that was hit hardest by Hurricane Lowell when it passed through on Monday and Tuesday.

The hurricane’s powerful winds and heavy rain damaged piers and ports, demolished beachfront buildings and knocked out power for a majority of Kauai. Two deaths also appear to have been linked to the storm, one on Oahu and one on Kauai, the authorities said.

The storm was the second hurricane to strike Hawaii in the past few weeks. In mid-August, Hurricane Lala drenched the Big Island with more than two feet of rain, washing away about 100 homes and killing three people.

In a statement on Thursday, Gov. Josh Green said the storm appeared to have caused more damage than Hurricane Iniki in September 1992. That storm devastated Kauai, killing at least 7 people and leaving $1.8 billion in damage.

Detailed assessments of the damage caused by Hurricane Lowell are still being conducted by local authorities. Some owners of oceanfront homes, hotels and businesses have reported damages, but the toll on the island is still largely unclear.

Gina Duarte, who lives in Waimea, on the west side of Kauai, said the storm surge from the hurricane had lifted boulders onto roads and yards and washed away the Waimea pier. Homes on the water were damaged, she said, and at least one road was washed out.

Ms. Duarte, whose home was without power, said on Wednesday that Kauai residents were trying to cope without air conditioning and the ocean breezes that usually cool the island.

“Everything is so wet, and it’s so hot,” she said.

Motorists dodged fallen trees and navigated intersections in Kauai without functioning traffic lights as emergency crews continued to clear roads and repair bridges. The highway on the Hanalei Bridge has been closed since Monday, cutting off communities on the north shore from the rest of the island.

Mr. Green said that the state needed help right away, before a full damage assessment could be completed. He noted that, in addition to the back-to-back hurricanes, Hawaii had been battered by another storm and an earthquake.

“We cannot wait for every damaged road, utility pole, harbor and public facility to be assigned a dollar value before asking the federal government to act,” he said.

In addition to Kauai, Mr. Green wrote in a letter to Mr. Trump, the state needed assistance to repair the state-owned commercial port on the island of Lanai, which was badly damaged and serves 3,000 residents. (Lanai is almost entirely owned by Larry Ellison, a billionaire who co-founded Oracle and who is a friend of Mr. Trump’s.)

Nearly 90 percent of Kauai’s 36,000 electric customers were without power in the initial aftermath of the storm. The Kauai Island Utility Cooperative, the power company for the island, said that “the assessment and restoration effort will be extensive.” By Thursday, only about 14,000 customers remained without electricity.

In Poipu, a tourist destination in Kauai, hotel pools were filled with sand, and some resorts and vacation rental homes were flooded.

Still, Kealiʻiheleua Makaloa of Koloa said on Wednesday, “We didn’t get too beaten up. Not too bad for us locals. We can survive.”

Shawn Hubler contributed reporting.

item.title: ‘You Know What Happens if You Don’t Vote’: 7 Takeaways From the G.O.P. Convention
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance was billed as the headliner of the second night of the Republican convention, but President Trump stole the show.

With a hug and a handshake, Mr. Vance exited stage right after his speech as Mr. Trump returned to the place he likes most — center stage — to make his final pitch of the convention to keep Republicans in power.

At one point Mr. Trump asked attendees to raise their right hands and pledge to him that he would vote with their family and friends. Dutifully, they did.

“You know what happens if you don’t vote?” Mr. Trump said. “You go to hell.”

The two-day rally in Dallas came as Mr. Trump’s approval has sagged below 40 percent and Republicans fear losing control of both the House and Senate. Republicans hoped the gathering would help energize a base beleaguered by high prices and the Iran war to turn out in droves. But the two days of red meat tossed from the stage seemed unlikely to satiate independent voters whose support has flagged.

Here are seven takeaways from the convention:

Mr. Vance arrived in Dallas widely considered the front-runner in the 2028 Republican presidential primary. His speech offered some early clues about how he might approach a campaign.

Mr. Vance focused on restoring the primacy of the traditional nuclear American family, a theme he has championed in the administration. He did not mention the war in Iran, an operation he has defended publicly but raised concerns about privately. But he issued a plea for conservatives not to abandon the White House over policy.

“Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater,” he urged.

Mr. Vance speaks in a far more scripted political style than Mr. Trump. He caught fire with the crowd when he snapped back at a protester who interrupted his remarks by waving Palestinian and Mexican flags. “My friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there,” he said.

But he failed to sustain the kind of enthusiasm that Mr. Trump commanded either night. Nor did he win anything beyond perfunctory praise from the president, who quickly ushered him off the stage.

As the balloons fell, it was the president alone, along with a tenor signing. Mr. Trump is not giving up his crown quite yet.

Mr. Trump has called affordability — a top buzzword for Democrats this year — a “hoax.” In his speech on Wednesday night, the president claimed that prices were on their way down. At the same time, he rolled out an audacious plan to address people’s concerns about costs: a huge cash giveaway.

He branded his dubious and detail-free plan to send $5,000 to every American adult a “Trump Dividend.”

But Mr. Trump was virtually the only one talking about it.

A day later, the splashy $1 trillion-plus plan barely made a ripple on the convention stage.

The president’s own son Donald Trump Jr. didn’t so much as mention it.

Neither did the speaker of the House.

Neither did the vice president.

Only Mr. Trump did.

If the president wants the dangled cash to be a major factor in the midterms, the rest of the Republican Party didn’t use the rest of the convention to sell it.

Forget about Nancy Pelosi.

In Dallas, Republicans made clear that the former House speaker has been dethroned from her decades-long position as the party’s favorite political villain.

Speaker after speaker assailed Hasan Piker, the leftist online streamer, and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, for pushing what they described as an extreme and anti-American agenda. Their images, including Mr. Piker’s naked torso, were broadcast on the jumbotron over the stadium. Even Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, who is a frequent target of the right, got less airtime.

At one point, Speaker Mike Johnson outlined the new rogues’ gallery of liberals — “Hasan Piker and Bernie Sanders and AOC and Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani” — while casting the rest of the Democratic Party as squishes who would succumb to them.

In their attacks on Mr. Piker and Mr. El-Sayed, several convention speakers embraced anti-Muslim rhetoric, including a promise popular among conservative activists to “ban Shariah law.”

“We must stand and defeat the Islamists,” said Senator Ted Cruz of Texas in his speech.

Republicans know that Mr. Trump is unpopular. They are banking on making Democrats unpopular, too — or at least unappealing and unelectable.

Over and over, speakers cast Democrats as out of the mainstream, frequently calling them socialists, communists and even worse. At times they stretched the truth. Democratic socialists might have won a number of Democratic primary victories since 2024, but no serious figure in the party is promoting communism.

“You guys are going to trigger the commies,” Donald Trump Jr. said at one point, as the crowd chanted “USA! USA! USA!”

Mr. Vance, in the closing of his speech, summed up the message so many had delivered before him over two days: “It’s about the party of common sense beating the party of the crazies.”

Six months ago, when it first emerged that Republicans were likely to pick Dallas for this convention, it was unclear whether Texas would wind up as a top midterm battleground.

It’s clear now.

A parade of speakers — from the president on down — used their precious time onstage to talk about Texas’s razor-close Senate race. They sought to boost Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general (even as Mr. Trump mocked his sartorial choices on back-to-back nights), and tear down James Talarico, the Democratic nominee. On the eve of the convention, Mr. Trump’s super PAC had reserved $10 million in ads to help Mr. Paxton.

“Tala-freako maybe tops the list,” Mr. Vance said of Mr. Trump’s nickname for Mr. Talarico.

But it wasn’t just the Senate race. Republicans gerrymandered the state in 2025 to create as many as five new safely Republican House seats. But Republicans running in several of those seats appeared at the convention, seeking a boost in regions that Mr. Trump won handily.

Mr. Trump has long been known as a master of the television audience. Not this time. An average of 2.5 million people tuned in to watch his Wednesday night speech on Fox News, one of the few major TV networks that aired the remarks in full, according to preliminary figures from Nielsen. That was an average prime-time audience for the network, based on the most recent quarterly statistics, and below the usual viewership for programs at that time.

In other words, no Trump bump.

To be fair, the president’s programming faced some steep competition. The first game of the National Football League season aired at the same time as his speech. The season’s second game was on Thursday during Mr. Vance’s and Mr. Trump’s speeches.

Parties in power traditionally attempt to expand their appeal in midterm elections through targeted outreach to independent voters. That was not the strategy charted by Mr. Trump and his allies in Dallas.

Only a handful of speakers offered any kind of outreach to moderate voters (one of those exceptions was Representative Mike Lawler of New York). Far more focused their remarks on stoking fears of Shariah law, transgender athletes and Democratic candidates who were repeatedly described as communists. Again and again, Mr. Trump begged his supporters to “pretend” that he would be on the ballot — an attempt to get enough of them out to prevent the usual losses for the party in power.

Mr. Trump and his allies are staking their chances on their ability to drive their own voters to the polls. At the top of the list are Trump loyalists who typically skip midterm elections.

Michael M. Grynbaum contributed reporting.

item.title: Indelible, Unshakable, but Now Fading: Views From Sept. 11, 2001
item.description:
A QUARTER-CENTURY later, the images remain so immediate and so raw, in the way that a movie you’ve seen many times before can still startle you. Dust-covered and tear-drenched, the photographs from Sept. 11 retain the power to take you back, and aback.

Each of these images tells its own chapter, but together, they form the 9/11 epic. The second plane about to pierce the south tower, confirming that the United States was under attack. The jagged and pulverized ruins of buildings that once symbolized world finance. The man exhausted from running for his life. The stillness of disbelief, conveyed by a tea set suddenly coated in gray. No matter where you were or are, there is an intimacy to these historic images that transcends the passage of time. A timelessness.

A universality. We are all caught between watching and averting our eyes. We are all searching in vain for who and what was lost. We are all just trying to hold it together.

Watching in shock as the towers fell, from a half-mile north of the World Trade Center.

The north tower at the beginning of the end.

Taking refuge, and a breather, in a Lower Manhattan deli after the first tower fell, but before the second collapse.

Later in the day, 7 World Trade Center collapsed.

Fleeing Lower Manhattan on the Brooklyn Bridge.

Word got to President George W. Bush during an event with schoolchildren in Florida.

The view from Brooklyn.

Tending to the wounded before the towers fell.

After the collapse.

An abandoned produce stand, covered in ash and frozen in time.

A woman calling her parents to let them know she was safe.

Sizing up the immeasurable scale of the destruction.

By the afternoon, the scale of the devastation began to become clearer.

A tea set caked in ash as if it were from Pompeii and not an apartment near ground zero.

A search for survivors, the morning after.

The funeral for a Fire Department chaplain who died in the attack.

Family members put up fliers in the hope their loved ones survived.

Smoke still rose from the rubble nearly a week after the attacks.

Saluting a fallen comrade at a funeral after the attacks. Hundreds of emergency responders were killed.

item.title: Vance, Eying 2028, Relishes the Spotlight at Trump’s Convention
item.description:
Republicans descended on Dallas this week with the ostensible aim of helping their candidates win midterm elections in a difficult political environment.

But for Vice President JD Vance, the moment offered a plum personal opportunity for an ambitious second-in-command. As he took the stage on Thursday night to deliver his keynote address, Mr. Vance made no effort to conceal how much he enjoyed the limelight.

“I got to say it’s pretty cool to hear a crowd that’s this fired up chant your name,” the vice president said, as supporters chanted his initials, JD. “Go ahead and do it again.”

The unusual two-day gathering of Republican candidates, activists and MAGA superfans in Dallas was styled to keep the focus squarely on President Trump. He demanded the party fund and organize the event, and speaker after speaker heaped praise on him. The president urged attendees to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and led them in a pledge of allegiance to himself.

But beneath the balloons and bedazzled MAGA apparel, Republicans were discussing the future of their party once Mr. Trump is no longer its leader. At the core of those conversations is the question of whether a party disassembled and remade in Mr. Trump’s image will transfer its support to his vice president, who has signaled interest in running to succeed him.

For his part, Mr. Vance on Thursday took some of his most concrete steps to try to position himself as the inheritor of Mr. Trump’s loyal base.

In his remarks, Mr. Vance sidestepped most of the thorniest issues dragging down his party. He only obliquely referenced the Iran war. He made no mention of tariffs that have exacerbated voters’ economic concerns, and he did not address Mr. Trump’s gambit to give voters $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress.

Instead, Mr. Vance placed a heavy emphasis on his own personal story, speaking more about his wife than any candidate running for office. The vice president drew on the recent birth of his fourth child and the first anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s death. And he appeared to relish playing the role of attack dog, at times lobbing provocative barbs against Democrats and gleefully dismissing a protester who interrupted his speech.

Mr. Vance’s scripted, more traditional political delivery cut a sharp contrast with the freewheeling and improvisational style of Mr. Trump. In fact, it was Mr. Vance’s unscripted response to the protester, who unfurled Mexican and Palestinian flags, that appeared to most energize the crowd.

“My friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there,” the vice president said, sending the crowd roaring. “I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”

Republicans say Mr. Vance, a onetime outspoken critic of Mr. Trump who later turned into a staunch supporter, remains the undisputed front-runner for the party’s presidential nomination — at one point, the crowd started chanting “48,” a reference to the 48th president. But they acknowledge he has work to do to consolidate support from Mr. Trump’s base, especially those who do not regularly vote or tune into politics.

“He has those relationships with the podcast hosts — Theo Von, Joe Rogan — who those guys listen to,” said Jack Posobiec, a far-right commentator and supporter of Mr. Vance. “The work that he’s going to have to do is convince them to come back in for 2028.”

To that end, Mr. Vance sought to make a direct appeal to skeptical and undecided voters — and specifically those who are unhappy with some of the administration’s policies.

“Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater,” he said. “Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”

He continued: “I’m not asking anybody to agree on every single policy of the administration. What I am asking you to do is recognize the contrast with the radicals and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months.”

The war with Iran has been a particularly sensitive topic for the vice president, who endorsed Mr. Trump in 2023, arguing that he would not lead the nation into any foreign wars. Mr. Vance privately opposed the conflict from the outset. He has publicly defended it even as parts of the base have revolted.

While jockeying for 2028 is already underway, the gathering in Dallas made clear Mr. Trump had no interest in relinquishing his ironclad grasp on the party. That has left Mr. Vance in the awkward position of trying to lay the groundwork for a potential presidential run without upsetting his mercurial boss.

Mr. Trump has suggested Mr. Vance is the front-runner for the nomination, but he has not formally endorsed him and has often asked aides and supporters who they think should succeed him. Some people close to Mr. Trump say the president could withhold his formal support for a while, preferring to let an “Apprentice”-style competition play out.

Mr. Trump often brings up Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, as a potential successor, though Mr. Rubio has said he would not run for president if Mr. Vance does. Mr. Rubio skipped the Dallas gathering because he was traveling in Latin America.

Others, including Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, who also spoke at the convention on Thursday, have signaled interest in potentially running for president in 2028.

The vice president also used the gathering to try to deepen his relationships with activists and donors. He bounced around state delegation breakfasts Thursday morning and appeared on “The Charlie Kirk Show” to honor Mr. Kirk on the first anniversary of his killing. (Erika Kirk, Mr. Kirk’s widow, who attended the convention’s first night, has already endorsed Mr. Vance for president.)

In the afternoon, Mr. Vance headlined a fund-raiser at the Ritz- Carlton in Dallas.

There, Mr. Vance attacked Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, for his past comments about the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, and joked that he had to add 95 minutes to his planned address Thursday night because he did not want to get shown up by Mr. Trump after the president’s lengthy speech Wednesday, according to two people in the room. Mr. Vance spoke for roughly 40 minutes at the convention.

Mr. Trump returned to the stage after Mr. Vance, offering him a handshake and hug. Before departing Dallas, Mr. Trump, who is known for his effusiveness, gave a review of Mr. Vance’s speech.

“He’s been a great vice president,” he told reporters before boarding Air Force One back to Washington. “I think he did a very good job.”

Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.
